content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
+ Good performance on temporal action detection benchmark.

+ The training speed of using pre-extracted feature is impressive.


Cons:
- The technical contribution is not novel enough.
  -  End-to-end training of temporal action detection can date back to SSN [1].
  - The IoU-balanced sampling is a rebranding of categorizing three types of proposals (positive, incomplete, background) in [1].
  - Gradient Sampling is a special case of Stochastic BP [2].

content.title: Authors Response to Reviewer xBZk
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments! Here we explain a few things.

> End-to-end training of temporal action detection can date back to SSN.
> 

In this paper, the emphasis is focused on efficient end-to-end training, not end-to-end training itself, which is also reflected in our paper title. Based on Table 4, ETAD is a memory-efficient TAD method that achieves state-of-the-art performance. 

> IoU-balanced sampling is a rebranding.
> 

All the sampling strategies described in section 3.3 are the existing methods, which may be proposed years ago. However, like the exploration of different samplings in MAE, the effect of different sampling strategies is unclear until the such study is conducted, which is meaningful for TAD. Sorry for the missed citation in label-guided strategies, we will add them in the revised version.

> Novelty of gradient sampling.
> 

Difference:

- Motivation. As illustrated in Fig1 in SBP, they find the gradients in the network are nearly the same for different video frames in the shallow layers but quite different in the deep layers. Thus they divide an arbitrary action recognition model into spatial layers and temporal layers (in section3.1 in SBP) and adopt selective gradient backpropagation for the spatial layers. Instead, in our paper,  we first observe the temporal redundancy in current end-to-end training methods in TAD, because TAD needs to extract tremendous snippet features to represent a video, and these snippets are highly redundant in semantics, thus we manage to backpropagate only a small portion of them. We particularly aim to reduce the temporal redundancy in end-to-end training in TAD.
- Sampling Strategy. In our work, we detailly propose two types of sampling strategies(heuristic, feature-guided) with a total of five approaches (random, grid, block, DPP, FPS). In SBP, they propose the gradient-norm-based sampling strategy. Our sampling strategy can be seen as a complementary of samplings in SBP.
- Sampling Ratio. In our work, we detailly study multiple sampling ratios and give the sampling ratio curve as in Fig4. In SBP, they only show three sampling ratios.

Similarities:

- Implementation. Though SBP only selectively backpropagates the spatial layers of a model, for TAD task, they treat the feature extraction backbone as the spatial layer and the action detector as the temporal layer, which results in nearly the same implementation as in our papers if the backbone is a CNN-like structure.

> Unclear conclusion.
> 

Respectfully, we summarize our conclusion as in abstract again, that, end-to-end can improve the TAD performance, and proposed gradient sampling and proposal sampling can achieve efficient end-to-end training. 

1. Using pre-extracted features, we confirm the proposal-level redundancy, and use proposal sampling to cut down both memory(16G to 1.2G in Fig. 4b) and training time (45mins to 6min in Fig. 4b). In this case, we can compare our method with other feature-based methods, and proves the effectiveness of proposed action detector.
2. Adopting end-to-end training can further improve the mAP, but it is memory-consuming. With end-to-end training, the mAP can be boosted from 36.06 to 36.85 with TSM-R50, but requires more than 500 GB, as shown in Fig. 4a.
3. Using gradient sampling can achieve memory-efficient end-to-end while maintaining a similar detection performance. As shown in Fig.4a, Table1, with gradient sampling, we can reduce the memory usage from 34GB per video to 11GB per video, while the mAP changes from 36.85 to 36.79, which achieves efficient end-to-end training.

We will add more comparisons with SBP and TALLFormer in the revised version. Thank you for your suggestion.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper investigates techniques to reduce the computational burden of the training of Temporal Action Detection approaches. This is done by proposing forms of sampling at two levels: 1) sampling of video snippets to train the encoder in an end-to-end fashion, 2) sampling of a subset of efficient action proposals. The two principles are applied to a generic TAD baseline. Experiments suggest that the proposed approach can achieve results comparable with state-of-the-art methods at lower computational costs for a range of snippet-level and proposal-level sampling procedures.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper overall reports an interesting investigation on the role of sampling to reduce the computational requirements when training TAD methods. Figure 4 nicely show how reasonable performance can be achieved with sampling ratios below 50% both for encoder gradient sampling and detector proposal sampling. 

Despite the comment above, I believe the paper still has some flaws which need to be addressed in order to make this a strong submission. In particular:
 - The experiments are based on the architecture shown in Figure 2. While all results are performed considering this architecture, it is not clear what is its rationale, in particular with respect to the feature enhancement module, which is not throughly described in the main paper. I would have expected the paper relying on a more general architecture (maybe a state-of-the-art one) to highlight the general applicability of the investigated principles. I would suggest to bring more discussion on the architecture in the main paper, so to explain the rationale behind it and why it is important to the proposed investigation.
 -  The results shown in Table 1 are a bit disappointing. I would have expected the proposed approach to achieve similar performance with much less computational requirements. Instead, the table seems to suggest that marginal gains can be obtained at similar training computational requirements as compared to state-of-the-art models (36.79 vs 36.54). Maybe I am just missing something from the table or discussion. Can the author clarify this point?
 - From Figure 3 and from the related discussion, it seems that the same heuristic sampling mechanism is applied both to gradient and proposal sampling, but it looks like the paper does not explore solutions in which one of the sampling mechanisms (e.g., random) is used for gradient selection and another one (e.g., grid) is used for proposals. Is this the case? Would such an investigation be relevant? Can the authors comment on that?
 - Table 2 is reporting 35.52 as the Avg. performance of TCANet with TSN features, while the paper also reports 37.56 when using SlowFast features, which seems to be on par with the results obtained with TSP. Can the authors comment on that?
 - Comparing Table 2 and Table 3, it seems that the approach has larger gains on THUMOS, however this point is not discussed in the paper. Could the authors comment on why this happens?
 - Similar to what observed with Table 1 a comparison between Table 4 and Table 2 does not highlight big gains when training end-to-end (less than 1% mAP comparing best models). I wonder if in this scenario, it is really so important to train end-to-end. Can the authors comment on this?
 - It would also be interesting to report memory requirements and training times in table 2 to show to what extent the proposed approach has a computational advantage with respect to other methods.

Other notes
 - In the abstract the paper states that operating on pre-extracted features leads to sub-optimal solutions. However, this does not seem to be shown experimentally. For instance, comparing Table 4 with Table 2, the gains seem to be minor. I would suggest to revise the statement.
 - Table 5 has a typo: feauture -> feature
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper could be improved in clarity. 
 - From a first read, it was not clear to me why forward-propagating all clips but only backward propagating some of the gradients would help. Then I thought that probably the TAL baseline still requires densely sampled per-clip features. Is my understanding correct? If so, I might have been confused by Figure 3, which does not mention that snippet-level sampling is only for gradients. If I am not correct, please let me know, but in either cases, I would suggest to revise the paper to make this point more explicit.
 - Section 3.2.2 reports that the relative efficiency gains brought by proposal sampling are more obvious with pre-extracted features, however, it is not clear to me where this is experimentally shown in the paper. Table 2 reports only modest improvements with respect to methods using pre-extracted features. Or maybe the reader should be referred to Figure 4? Can the authors clarify this in the paper?
 - When the reader gets to Section 4.2 it is not clear which sampling mechanisms have been adopted in the end for comparison. This becomes clearer later when reading section 4.3. I would suggest switching the order of these two sections.
 - If I understood correctly, when using pre-extracted features, only the proposal sampling mechanism is used. Is this the case? If so, this should probably be better highlighted in Section 4.2 when discussing Table 2.

Also, many important details are reported in the appendix rather than in the main paper. In particular, the architecture reported in Figure 2 should be presented in details in the main paper including ablations. Reading Figure 2 in the main paper, it is not clear what is the role of the feature enhancement module and the reverse order "~" operator.
content.summary_of_the_review: I overall liked the investigation carried out in the paper, but I believe many points need revision to make the submission stronger, as reported in the boxes above.

content.title: Authors Response to Reviewer YiNf
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for the effort of detailed reviews and comments! Here we clarify some comments.

> Why uses a specific architecture in Figure2 instead of more general architecture?
> 

The complete approach of the proposed method follows “action detector + proposal sampling + snippet sampling”. Action detector aims to have a good detection performance (36.10 in Figure 4b), while it is not time and memory efficient (45 mins and 16.1G in Figure 4b). Then with proposal sampling, we reduce the training time to 6 mins and memory to 1.3G (Figure 4b), but maintain nearly the same mAP (36.06). Furthermore, with snippet sampling, we can achieve memory-efficient end-to-end training (Table 4) with higher performance (36.79). Therefore, the proposed architecture is the study baseline and also critical for high-performance TAD, and it can also benefit the TAD community as a strong detector. If using more general architecture, this would limit this paper’s contribution.

> Marginal results in Table 1.
> 

First, as shown in Table1, adopting end-to-end can at most boost the mAP from 36.13 to 36.85 in our case, and this is achieved by Completely End-to-End Training which uses 34GB memory per video. The methods listed in the middle of Table1 should approximate the 36.85 as much as possible, while using less memory. Since ETAD and feature bank approach all use 30% snippet for backpropagation, thus the memory is nearly the same (11GB), but our performance is better (36.79 vs 36.54). And our 36.79 is very close to the Completely End-to-End Training(36.85).

> Investigation of more combinations of sampling strategies.
> 

Though random and grid sampling perform similarly in proposal sampling and snippet sampling, we will put this result on the supplementary material for reference. Thank you for your suggestion.

> TCANet with slowfast feature.
> 

It is a fair comparison in TAD only if you are using the same pre-extracted features or video encoders. TCANet reports the results using TSN features, which we also compared at the top of Table 2 (35.53 vs 36.06). The author of TCANet did not release their slowfast feature on ANET, thus it is not easy to reproduce the same features, since one may use the different settings of pretraining, depth, frame resolution, etc to extract features. So there is no need to compare with TCANet if one uses slowfast feature, and the other one uses TSP feature, though the performances are similar.

> Larger gains on THUMOS than ANET.
> 

Since ANET has 4k validation videos and THUMOS has only 213 validation videos, thus the common improvements on THUMOS are larger than ANET. Such a trend also happens in other methods, such as BMN, and TCANet.

> Marginal gains with end-to-end training.

First, it is not easy to improve 1% mAP for TAD, especially on large-scale ActivityNet dataset after years of studies. Second, with TSM-R50 backbone, we boost the mAP from 36.06 to 36.79 (+0.73). For comparison, LoFi (NerIPS2022) uses multi-stage end-to-end training to improve the mAP from 34.26 to 34.96 (+0.70). Thus our results on end-to-end learning are reasonable. We think if using longer training epochs (now only 6) and stronger data augmentation, the performance can be further increased.

> Report the training time and memory consumption of other methods.
> 

Thanks for your advice. In Appendix D, we also compare our training time and memory usage with BMN and TCANet. In Figure 1, we also compare VSGN and G-TAD. We will try to reproduce more methods and collect all the results together.

> Feature extraction in TAD
> 

Yes, it is still the standard approach in TAD to extract dense clip-level features (or called snippet features), which is also used in this paper. Figure 3 tried to explain different sampling strategies on proposal map or snippet sequence. We will improve the clarity of this figure.

> Efficiency of proposal sampling.
> 

Since the end-to-end training (5.5G per video x batch size 16) requires much more GPU memory than feature-based training (total 16G without proposal sampling). If adopting the proposal sampling, both memory can be reduced, but the reduction in end-to-end training seems not that obvious, because the majority of computation is spent on the video encoder. This conclusion is shown in Figure 4 (a and b), but I will add the explanation in the revised version.

> Suggestions on writing.
> 

Thanks for your suggestion. Section 4.2 all uses the random sampling. We will switch 4.2 and 4.3 for better reading. Besides, it is true that only proposal sampling is adopted in pre-extracted feature experiments. I will add the explanation in the revised version.

Thanks for your effort and suggestions again!

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach for efficient temporal action detection (ETAD) based on sampling: both at the snippet and proposal level. The main motivation of this work is to reduce the memory requirement and training time for end-to-end training of temporal action detection (TAD) models. Experiments are conducted on ActivityNet 1.3 and THUMOS'14 with good results compared with current methods. The proposed ETAD is more efficient and requires less GPU memory while maintain a similar performance (mAP). Written presentation is clear and easy to read.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength
- The proposed approach, ETAD, is efficient (requires less memory, trained end-to-end, faster training time) while still maintain the similar performance (mAP).
- The ablation are comprehensive: different sampling methods are ablated at both snippet and proposal level.
- Written presentation is with high clarity and easy to read.

# Weakness
- The novelty is limited due to [a]. The authors of [a] proposed  Stochastic Backpropagation (SBP) for efficient video training. Note that Gradient Sampling (termed in this paper) is very similar SBP (technically the same) when it is applied to tree model (see Fig 3a of [a]). In [a], SBP was experimented on Kinetics, EPIC-Kitchens, and THUMOS'14. So SBP was previously proposed for both video classification and TAD. The difference in ETAD, may be on the proposal-level sampling which is specifically applied to TAD problem. Please discuss the difference w.r.t [a] and (if possible) discuss the significant of proposal sampling quantitative and qualitative since it is the only novel component in ETAD compared with SBP [a].

- Given [a] was proposed before, the reviewer wonder if the technical contributions of ETAD are enough for publications? Here is a head-to-head comparison. First, SBP was proposed for efficient training of long-video, demonstrated on both video classification and TAD, SBP is designed to work for both tree model and graph model. On the other hand, ETAD (this paper) tries to propose gradient sampling and proposal sampling for TAD. Note that gradient sampling is the same as SBP, so the only new component in ETAD is proposal sampling. ETAD is only designed for temporal action detection. To the authors, in the rebuttal, please discuss how significant the contributions of ETAD w.r.t. SBP [a].


[a] Cheng et al., Stochastic Backpropagation: A Memory Efficient Strategy for Training Video Models, CVPR 2022.

content.title: Authors Response to Reviewer LYuD
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for the effort of detailed reviews and comments! We appreciate your approval of the efficiency and efficacy of our method, and detailed ablations and writings.

> Comparison of our gradient sampling approach with other methods.
> 

Here, we mainly discuss the similarities and differences between our method with SBP (CVPR2022).

Difference:

- Motivation. As illustrated in Fig1 in SBP, they find the gradients in the network are nearly the same for different video frames in the shallow layers but quite different in the deep layers. Thus they divide an arbitrary action recognition model into spatial layers and temporal layers (in section3.1 in SBP) and adopt selective gradient backpropagation for the spatial layers. Instead, in our paper,  we first observe the temporal redundancy in current end-to-end training methods in TAD, because TAD needs to extract tremendous snippet features to represent a video, and these snippets are highly redundant in semantics, thus we manage to backpropagate only a small portion of them. We particularly aim to reduce the temporal redundancy in end-to-end training in TAD.
- Sampling Strategy. In our work, we detailly propose two types of sampling strategies(heuristic, feature-guided) with a total of five approaches (random, grid, block, DPP, FPS). In SBP, they propose the gradient-norm-based sampling strategy. Our sampling strategy can be seen as a complementary of samplings in SBP.
- Sampling Ratio. In our work, we detailly study multiple sampling ratios and give the sampling ratio curve as in Fig4. In SBP, they only show three sampling ratios.

Similarities:

- Implementation. Though SBP only selectively backpropagates the spatial layers of a model, for TAD task, they treat the feature extraction backbone as the spatial layer and the action detector as the temporal layer, which results in nearly the same implementation as in our papers if the backbone is a CNN-like structure.

To be honest, the first submission of this paper is before the release of SBP’s arxiv version. Still, we acknowledge that we miss the comparison between them in the paper. We will add a detailed comparison of our method with SBP in the improved version. 

> Novelty of ETAD.
> 

We emphasize the novelty of ETAD from 3 aspects.

1. we propose gradient sampling to reduce the memory limitation for end-to-end training in TAD.
2. we propose the proposal sampling to reduce the computation complexity for the action detector. 
3. we propose a simple but effective action detector for TAD.

Though novelty1 seems to overlap with the SBP paper, we still want to emphasize the value of novelty2 and novelty3. 
1. The proposal sampling is the first to explicitly point out that dense enumerated proposals are redundant for training an action detector, which can be helpful for many state-of-the-art methods, such as BMN(ICCV2019), GTAD(CVPR2020), etc. We also emphasize that proposal sampling can visibly reduce the computation complexity of an action detector, given the pre-extracted features, proposal sampling successfully reduces the training time from 45mins to 6mins, and cut down the memory usage from 16GB to 1.2GB. Such training efficiency is not achieved before in state-of-the-art TAD methods. 
2. In this paper, we propose a cascade action detector (described in 3.1 and appendix A), which achieves state-of-the-art performance on TAD benchmarks (table2,3). A comprehensive ablation of the action detector itself is also conducted in Appendix C. Such an action detector showed the best performance on the ActivityNet dataset till now. With our proposal sampling strategy, even without end-to-end training, our action detector can beat most state-of-the-art methods. 
3. On the largest TAD dataset HACS, without end-to-end training (only novelty 2 and 3), we achieve the current best performance, which surpasses the previous SOTA which is the combination of two different networks.

Therefore, from the aspect of method novelty, we think our sampling-based approach to reduce the computation is novel and important for the TAD community. From the aspect of technical contributions, the sampling implementation and proposed action detector are also important and helpful for wider audiences in the TAD community.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposed ETAD, an efficient temporal action detection method. Most existing TAD methods used pre-extracted features, since they require heavy GPU consumption when training the feature extractor end to end with the TAD model. While, training an e2e network is preferable for boosting performance. This work alleviates the problem by proposing sampling strategies including snippet level and proposal level sampling. In the snippet level, they reduce number of snippets for gradient computation. In the proposal level, they reduce the proposal number to reduce redundancy. As a result, they are able to reduce significant GPU consumption with better model performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. training TAD models end to end is a more elegant strategy and has good potential to improve results. However, this cannot be done with limited GPU resources. This work alleviated the problem by proposing sampling based strategies. 

2. the method is simple yet effective, showing SOTA performance with less GPU consumption.

3. the paper is well written and well motivated.

Weaknesses:
Thumos and Activitynet1.3 have different actions per video. For example, each Thumos video has around 15-16 actions, while activitynet1.3 has 1.5 actions averagely per video. Given this fact, activitynet should be more "redundant", right? Why do you use the same sampling rate for both? 

Table 4 showed e2e results of activitynet. Where are the results of Thumos?

content.title: Authors Response to Reviewer W5ar
content.comment:
Thank you for your positive evaluation of our work, especially for appreciating our motivation for efficient end-to-end training in TAD and the proposed solution.

> Table 4 showed e2e results of ActivityNet. Where are the results of Thumos?

Please see Appendix E for our end-to-end training results on THUMOS. To be clear, since we are using a shorter clip length, lower resolution, and only RGB modality, the performance is expected to be lower than the state-of-the-art methods. Still, the performance beats the other end-to-end training methods (eg. SBP) on THUMOS (mAP@0.5, 44.40 vs 31.46).

> Why do you use the same sampling rate for both?

There are two reasons for this choice. 
1. Though THUMOS has a larger amount of actions per video than AcitivtyNet, the video length of THUMOS is also much larger than AcitivityNet. Since we use sliding window on THUMOS videos yet rescaling to a fixed length on ActivityNet dataset, which is the typical data processing approach in TAD, the ground truth actions of a network input (not a video), are nearly the same in the two datasets. Therefore, using the same sampling rate won’t affect the performance too much. 
2. From the table11 and figure, we can find that the performance is not sensitive to the sampling ratio if the ratio is larger than 10%. Thus, we empirically set the sampling rate as 30% on both datasets.
